structured_output.summary: Scope: the D3 working diff in /private/tmp/medfit-d1.3jrA2K/medfit against a11c63b, read statically only. No tests were run, nothing was edited, and nothing was installed or simulated. I found no ship-blocking defect in the D3 code. Raw cardinality is computed from the parser's `length(p$factors)` before any grid is built, with an overflow guard and an unchanged `> 64L` refusal. Execution order and `which.min` tie-breaking are untouched. Structural IDs and a strict `identical(x$branch_map, .sem_branch_map(x$constraints))` check are added in `.sem_valid_outcome`. The remaining findings are clause-to-test evidence gaps against PROPOSAL D3 and one small behavioural risk that I inferred from the code and did not run. None of this is a global acceptance claim. T5, D4/D5 and the real-case evidence stay open. I did not review any legacy D1/D2 behaviour except where D3 touches it.

findings.title: Mocked tests do not prove the raw-to-canonical mapping is stable under factor permutation, collision-free, or fully tamper-checked
findings.body: The PROPOSAL D3 PASS requires 'overlapping/duplicate product constraints and factor permutations'. The only permutation test (test-sem-branch-map.R:68-69) reverses the order of constraint rows and asserts `expect_setequal` on the IDs. It does not check the following. (a) Reordering the factors inside one product row (`a1*b1` versus `b1*a1`) leaves the ID set unchanged. (b) That reordering also changes the grid order, so the raw-row-to-ID alignment is not asserted anywhere. (c) `unique_count` is not rechecked after permuting. (d) Two different restriction sets never share an ID (collision or encoding ambiguity). `encode()` at R/sem-outcomes.R:28 is length-prefixed, but nothing exercises labels containing digits or ':'. Tamper evidence is similarly thin: test-sem-branch-map.R:36 forges only `raw_to_canonical[1]`. Forged `raw_count`, `factor_counts`, `unique_count` and `state` are covered only implicitly by `identical()`, with no assertion.
findings.recommendation: Add assertions for: single-row factor reordering; the per-raw-row ID vector under a factor permutation (a bijection between raw rows, not just setequal); an ID-distinctness control using adversarial labels; and one tamper case per `branch_map` field.

findings.title: Cardinality boundary and overflow controls are narrower than the D3 PASS wording
findings.body: test-sem-branch-map.R:2 checks 63/64/65 only as a single-factor vector `.sem_raw_count(n)`. It does not test multi-factor products at the boundary (c(8,8)=64, c(8,9)=72), and it does not test the finite-but-above-integer.max range (for example 2^31 to 2^53). In that range `.sem_raw_count` (R/sem-outcomes.R:11) returns a double, and `sprintf('%s', raw_count)` at R/sem-fit.R:276 renders scientific notation such as '1.099512e+12'. The only overflow case is `rep(2L, 2000L)` giving Inf (line 3). So the `count <= .Machine$integer.max` branch and the `count > xmax / n` guard are exercised only at the extremes. The 63 and 65 boundaries are never driven through `.sem_fit_branches`; only 32, 64 and 128 are, at lines 22 and 48.
findings.recommendation: Add multi-factor boundary and mid-range finite-large cases. Pin the refusal message format and the type of `enumeration$required` (integer, double, Inf).

findings.title: Tie-order evidence is weak: the varying-score case is a unique minimum, and the mock records only constraint lhs
findings.body: The 'ties' claim rests on constant payload `f`, where `which.min` returns the first row (test-sem-branch-map.R:30-32). The varying case (lines 39-46) uses f = c(4,1,3,2), which has a unique minimum at row 2, so it is not a tie. No case ties at a non-first position, and no case ties between rows that share a canonical ID. The mock at lines 14-21 records only `parsed$constraints$lhs`. It ignores rhs and every other argument (n_starts, control, weights, se_type and the rest), so 'unchanged execution' is shown only as an lhs call sequence. This is a test-strength gap, not a code defect.
findings.recommendation: Add a tie at a non-first position, including between duplicate-canonical rows. Also assert that the full argument list passed to `.sem_fit_syntax` is unchanged.

findings.title: `.sem_outcome` now runs the constraint parser on every node, so a parser error could mask the original fit error (inferred)
findings.body: D3 adds `branch_map = .sem_branch_map(constraints)` inside `.sem_outcome` (R/sem-outcomes.R:152). `.sem_outcome` is also called on error and cleanup paths: R/sem-fit.R:278 and the branch ledger fallback around R/sem-fit.R:327. `.sem_branch_map` calls `.sem_zero_product_rows`, which parses expressions. If that call throws on a malformed or odd constraint row, the throw would replace the typed `medfit_sem_unresolved` condition and its ledger. The constraints are mostly pre-parsed earlier in the same call, so the risk is low. I did not run this and no test covers it. The extra per-node parsing cost is also new.
findings.recommendation: Either build `branch_map` only for union nodes, or wrap it in a guard that records an error state instead of throwing. Add a test that a parser failure in the map does not mask the original typed condition.

next_steps: Add the missing permutation, collision, boundary and tamper assertions to tests/testthat/test-sem-branch-map.R, then run the D3 tests, test-sem-outcomes.R, test-sem-branches.R and test-sem-edge-grid.R. I did not run them.
Decide whether `branch_map` belongs only on union nodes, or is guarded against parser throws.
Keep T5 UNACCEPTED. D4, D5 and the real-case evidence remain open.
